raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis on high-dose infliximab was diagnosed with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis at two weeks postpartum. Her unusual case involved vertical transmission of histoplasmosis to her child and has been previously reported . Given fever and systemic symptoms with nodular infiltrate on chest imaging and laboratory evidence of anemia and hepatitis, she was treated with intravenous Amphotericin B for two weeks and then transitioned to itraconazole capsules. Initial urine histoplasma antigen (UHAg) was >19 ng/ml, which is above the limit of quantification (LoQ) for the MiraVista assay used (scale of results: Negative; Positive - below the LoQ <0.4 ng/ml; Positive - 0.4-19 ng/ml; Positive - above the LoQ >19 ng/ml; Histoplasma Quantitative Enzyme Immunoassay). Her itraconazole levels were monitored every 3-4 months and were in therapeutic range throughout her treatment, and she clinically improved [Figure 1].
At her 12-month follow-up visit, UHAg was measured at 1.81 ng/ml. Itraconazole was continued due to her significant immunosuppression at diagnosis, high antigen levels at diagnosis, and persistently positive UHAg. UHAg subsequently increased at month fifteen to 3.07 ng/ml. During the discussion of results, the patient noted that she was subjectively volume depleted, resulting in a low-volume, concentrated-appearing urine specimen. She increased water intake and provided a repeat sample seven days later that showed a 'Negative' UHAg result [Figure 1].
Histoplasmosis is a common fungal infection in the Ohio and Mississippi River Valley regions caused by inhalation of Histoplasma capsulatum with a wide range of clinical manifestations. Immunosuppressed patients are at higher risk for the development of progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. While culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis, its sensitivity is limited. Thus, antigen detection assays utilizing serum, urine, bronchoalveolar lavage, and cerebrospinal fluid have emerged as an effective tool for the diagnosis of active infection.
While UHAg testing has a high sensitivity of 91-95%, unexpected variability of UHAg during monitoring of disease has been reported. Fluctuating urine concentrations have been hypothesized as a cause of this variability; however, no study has directly evaluated the physiologic concentration of urine and effects on antigenuria. One study, conducted to evaluate if ultrafiltration of false-negative UHAg samples improved detection rates, concluded that ultrafiltration increases antigen detection in previously false-negative samples. This research supports the theory that dilution of urine may result in reduced sensitivity of antigen detection. Given the effects of urinary concentration on antigen detection, we hypothesize that the variability of this patient's UHAg may be related to her volume status and urine concentration. Alternatively, it is possible that this variability may have been a laboratory error.
If levels of urine antigen do vary based on concentration as has been suggested in this case report and in the ultrafiltration study, volume status should be considered when interpreting UHAg testing, which can be of considerable importance in both inpatient and outpatient populations. Urine dilution may lead to more false-negative results than previously appreciated, and conversely, increased urinary concentration may lead to spuriously elevated results, complicating interpretation of treatment response. Determining whether urine dilution affects antigenuria to a clinically significant degree is especially important since many patients with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis are volume resuscitated when initial testing occurs. Further study is warranted to determine if urine concentration affects urine antigen levels and its subsequent clinical significance.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old postpartum woman with ulcerative colitis on high-dose infliximab presented 2 weeks after delivery with fever and systemic symptoms, and was subsequently monitored over 15 months for fluctuating urine Histoplasma antigen levels.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed at 2 weeks postpartum with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (complicated by vertical transmission to her infant), treated with 2 weeks of IV amphotericin B followed by oral itraconazole capsules with clinical resolution. At 12-month and 15-month follow-up visits, her quantitative urine Histoplasma antigen (UHAg) unexpectedly rose from 1.81 ng/mL to 3.07 ng/mL during a period of subjective volume depletion before turning negative 7 days later after oral hydration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ulcerative colitis treated with high-dose infliximab; 2 weeks postpartum at initial diagnosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for fever and systemic symptoms; at 15-month follow-up, clinically improved on oral itraconazole but reported subjective dehydration/concentrated urine.

objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed anemia and hepatitis; initialchest imaging showed nodular pulmonary infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial MiraVista quantitative urine Histoplasma antigen (UHAg) EIA monitoring: >19 ng/mL (above limit of quantification) at initial diagnosis; 1.81 ng/mL at 12 months; 3.07 ng/mL at 15 months in a concentrated low-volume specimen; and Negative (<0.4 ng/mL) on repeat testing 7 days later after increased oral water intake (with consistently therapeutic serum itraconazole levels).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Postpartum progressive disseminated histoplasmosis in a patient on infliximab, with spurious/physiologic elevation of follow-up urine Histoplasma antigen caused by urinary concentration/dehydration. Confirmation: Initial UHAg >19 ng/mL resolving to negative after 2 weeks of IV amphotericin B, 15 months of therapeutic oral itraconazole, and oral rehydration confirming that the 15-month UHAg bounce (3.07 ng/mL) was secondary to concentrated urine. Plan & clinical course: Completed 2 weeks of IV amphotericin B and prolonged oral itraconazole therapy with full clinical recovery and conversion to negative urine Histoplasma antigen.
